the cytotoxic effects of smoke from combustion of materials used in building and transport industry on human lung derived cells have been investigated.
the combustion products of the materials studied are cytotoxic to human lung cells.

the development of a new approach to evaluate fire toxicity of materials and products.
understanding the effects of combustion toxicants on human lung cells.
the potential health hazard from combustion of materials used in building and modern transportation interiors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the combustion of the selected polymers and composite materials has an adverse effect on the viability and morphology of human lung derived cells, and that the cytotoxicity and the morphological changes were dependent on the type of polymer and composite materials used.
the smoke from the combustion of polymers and composites is toxic.
the toxicity ranking of the materials studied is dependent on the test method employed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the toxicity ranking from most toxic to least toxic was: PVC>PP>MFP>FRPs>PC>HDPE.
PVC is the most toxic of the materials studied, followed by PP and HDPE.
the toxicity of combustion products from polymers is dependent on the chemical composition of the polymer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the combustion of polymers can have significant effects on human cells and the toxicity of the combustion products is dependent on the polymer type.

the use of the NRU and ATP assays in conjunction with the morphological assessment of the effects of combustion toxicants in human lung cells can provide a better understanding of the toxicity of smoke products.
the use of FRP and MFB in building and transport applications is not a significant health risk to occupants.
